sheet.name: Maren
sheet.opening: Maren stands in the courtyard of the Temple of the Anvil Father as evening shadows lengthen across the stone. The mine entrance was sealed at sunrise — she watched the masons lay the final bricks, heard the council's proclamation that the Old North Works were closed forever. Brakka never came back. They had served together for six years, shared meals in the refectory, traded stories of the mountain's moods. Now Brakka is gone, and Maren needs answers. Hessa is in her quarters, and Maren is heading there now, the miner's note burning in her mind — the one the miners left with the prior before they went down, warning of an old door that should never have been opened.
sheet.personality: I see omens in every event and action. The gods try to speak to us, we just need to listen. Nothing can shake my optimistic attitude.

Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Town Council of Greyhollow; added 2 relationships to Town Council of Greyhollow

The world is old, and the mountains remember everything that was ever buried in them. The Frostpeak range runs north to south like a wall of grey stone, and the people who live in its valleys have always dug into its bones for iron and silver. The Anvil Father, they say, forged the mountains themselves, and the dwarves who worship him have tended the deep places since before the humans came down from the north.

Brakka Ironvein is one of those dwarves. Six years ago she took the temple's oath and stood guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town carved into the western face of the Frostpeaks. She has kept the peace, watched the processions, and listened to the mountain groan through the stone walls. She knows the mine's sounds better than most.

Three days ago, three miners went down into the old north workings — tunnels sealed a generation ago after a collapse that no one in town likes to talk about. None of them came back. Last night a fourth man, Greth Oremine, stumbled out of the dark alone. He babbled about lights that walk and eyes that watch from deep stone, then died before dawn with his fingernails broken from clawing at the mine door.

Now Brakka stands at the mine mouth in the late afternoon light. The entrance is a mouth of rough-hewn stone, half-hidden by a wooden trestle and a rusted winch. Beyond it, the tunnel slopes downward into blackness. The lantern in her hand burns steady. The wind from below is cold and smells of wet stone and something else — something faintly metallic, like old blood on a blade.

Sunrise is tomorrow. After that, the council will seal the entrance forever.

What does Brakka do?

I check the ground at the mine mouth for tracks and signs of who has passed through recently, then tie a length of rope off to the winch trestle so I have a lifeline back. Once that's set, I raise my lantern and start down the slope slowly, shield up, listening for anything beyond the wind.

You tie your rope to the winch trestle, looping it twice and knotting it secure. Fifty feet of hempen rope should give you something to follow if the dark plays tricks on you.

The tunnel descends at a steady angle, the walls rough-hewn stone that your darkvision picks out in shades of grey. The lantern casts warm light ahead of you, pushing back the blackness. Timber supports brace the ceiling at intervals, some old and black with age, others newer — the three miners must have replaced a few before they went deeper. The air is cold and damp, and that metallic smell grows stronger as you descend.

You walk for ten minutes, your boots echoing on the stone floor. The tunnel bends once to the left, then continues down. The rope trails behind you, a lifeline to the world above. Ahead, the light of your lantern reaches only so far before the dark swallows it.

You move forward carefully, shield raised, lantern sweeping the walls and floor. At the deep gouge where the scratches end, you crouch and study the dust. Near the knee-marks, you find something: a small leather pouch, its drawstring pulled loose. Inside, you find a few copper pieces, a piece of chalk, and a folded note. The note reads, in a miner's rough hand: "Told ye we shouldn't have opened the old door. Hessa said seal it for a reason. But the vein runs deep and the council wants the ore." The note is dated three days ago.

You stand and look ahead. The tunnel continues its curve, and with your keen eyes you pick out what's been growing stronger: the walls here are different. Veins of a dark, almost black mineral run through the grey stone, branching like roots. The metallic smell comes from these veins — a sharp, iron-and-copper tang that coats your tongue. The mineral catches the lantern light with a faint, oily sheen, but it doesn't look like any ore you've seen in six years of guarding the temple's stores.

The miners' prints continue past the gouge, but they're erratic now — some steps forward, some back, as if the men had argued or panicked. Then, about forty feet ahead, the tunnel opens into a wider space. You can see where the old stonework ends and something else begins: a rough breach in the wall, as if someone had broken through into an older, natural cavern. Timber from the old seal lies splintered on the ground.

The air from that breach is colder, and the metallic smell is almost overpowering now. From somewhere beyond, you hear a sound — faint, but unmistakable. It's a low, rhythmic hum, like stone vibrating against stone.

What do you do?

I pocket the note and the chalk, then use the chalk to mark an arrow at the gouge so I can find my way back. I creep toward the breach, keeping to the wall with shield up, and stop at the edge to listen to the hum and peer in without stepping through, holding my lantern low to limit how far its light shows.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

Evening shadows stretch across the courtyard of the Temple of the Anvil Father as Maren steps out of the refectory. The air is cold, carrying the scent of woodsmoke from the town below. The mine entrance was sealed at sunrise — she watched the masons lay the final bricks, heard the council's proclamation that the Old North Works were closed forever.

Brakka never came back.

They had served together for six years, shared meals in this very courtyard, traded stories of the mountain's moods. Brakka had gone down three days ago to find the missing miners, and yesterday Greth Oremine had stumbled out babbling about lights that walk. Then nothing. Now the mine is sealed, and Brakka is gone.

Hessa is in her quarters in the temple's east wing. The prior has been silent since the sealing, spending the day in prayer and contemplation. But Maren knows the old dwarf has answers — the miner's note that Hessa gave her this morning proves it. The miners had left it with the prior before they went down, warning that they shouldn't have opened the old door, that Hessa herself had said to seal it for a reason.

Maren's hand rests on the holy symbol at her chest. She needs to speak with Hessa, to understand what that door was, why it was sealed, and what took Brakka.

The temple's stone corridors are dim in the evening light, the lamps not yet lit. Hessa's quarters are down the east hall, past the shrine room where incense still burns.

Then you continue down the east hall to Hessa's door. The wood is old, darkened with age and oil from many hands. You knock gently.

"Maren," she says, her voice rough. She steps back and opens the door wider. "Come in."

Her quarters are sparse — a narrow bed, a writing desk covered in papers and old books, a small shrine to the Anvil Father with a single unlit candle. The air smells of old paper and cold stone.

Hessa closes the door and turns to face you. Her eyes fall to the note in your hand.

"You've come about the door," she says. It's not a question.

She moves to her desk and sits heavily in a wooden chair, gesturing for you to sit on the bed. She folds her hands in her lap and looks at you for a long moment.

"Your friend Brakka went down there because I asked her to," Hessa says quietly. "The miners — Torvin, Durgan, and Kael — they went against my counsel. She pauses, her jaw tightening.

Hessa nods slowly. "I thought you'd ask that." She opens the book and turns the pages with practiced care. The parchment is brittle, the ink faded to brown.

"Here," she says, pointing to a passage. "The account of the Collapse. It says the survivors were found unconscious in the main tunnel, not in the cavern itself. The lights... they didn't follow the miners back through the breach. They stayed in the cavern."

She turns another page. "There's mention of a ventilation shaft — an old one, carved to air out the cavern after the incident. It was sealed too, but less thoroughly. The records say it's 'above the old adit, behind the masonry.' The old adit is a smaller entrance higher up the mountain face, abandoned centuries ago. It's overgrown now, but it might still be passable."

Hessa looks up at you. "The records also say the survivors were found with their hands burned, as if they'd touched hot stone. And that the lights retreated when the temple priests came with consecrated oil and blessed the tunnel. The Anvil Father's light, they called it."

She closes the book and meets your eyes. "There's no map, Maren. No clear instructions. Only fragments. But if there's another way in, it's through that old adit. And if the lights fear the Anvil Father's light, then you'll need more than a lantern."

She stands and moves to her shrine, lighting the unlit candle. "Take this," she says, handing you a small vial of oil from the shrine. "It's been blessed. Consecrated to the Anvil Father. It won't last long, but it might buy you time."

She pauses, then adds, "The old adit is a two-hour climb up the mountain face from here. If you leave now, you might reach it before dawn."

Hessa nods solemnly. "I'll see to it, Maren. The Anvil Father go with you."

You pack the rope, the second lantern, the consecrated oil, and the miner's note. Your warhammer hangs at your belt, your light crossbow loaded and ready. You keep your shield close and move quietly, the metal gear muffled against your chain mail.

The climb is steep and cold. The path winds up the mountain face, switchbacking through scree and loose stone. The wind cuts through your cloak, and the stars above are sharp and bright in the winter sky. Your Guidance fades as you climb, but the Anvil Father's presence lingers in your mind.

After two hours of steady climbing, you reach the old adit. It's a narrow opening in the rock face, half-hidden by dead brush and lichen. The masonry Hessa mentioned is still there — old bricks, crumbling with age, sealing a ventilation shaft above the entrance. The wood of the original door frame is rotted away, and the stone around it is stained with moisture.

A figure waits nearby, huddled in a heavy cloak. He stands as you approach, his breath visible in the cold air.

"Maren?" he says. "I'm Dorin. Hessa sent word." His face is lined with worry, and his eyes keep moving toward the sealed entrance. "I've been up here before, checking the shafts. But I've never gone in. Not since... not since Torvin went down."

He gestures to the old adit. "The ventilation shaft is behind that masonry. It's narrow, but passable. It leads down to the cavern where... where they found the blackvein."

sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.
sheet.ac_note: Chain Mail 16 + shield 2; disadvantage on Stealth

sheet.proficiencies: All armor, Battleaxes, Handaxes, Light hammers, Martial Weapons, Shields, Simple Weapons, Smith's Tools, Warhammers
attacks: Longsword: +4 to hit, 1d8+4 slashing (Dueling +2 included: one-handed, no other weapon); 1d10+2 two-handed (versatile)
Crossbow, light: +2 to hit, 1d8 piercing; range 80/320 (ammunition, loading, two-handed)
Unarmed strike: +4 to hit, 3 bludgeoning
features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.
Dwarven Combat Training: You have proficiency with the battleaxe, handaxe, light hammer, and warhammer.
Tool Proficiency: You gain proficiency with the artisan's tools of your choice: smith's tools, brewer's supplies, or mason's tools.
Dwarven Toughness: Your hit point maximum increases by 1, and it increases by 1 every time you gain a level.

Fighting Style: You adopt a particular style of fighting as your specialty. Choose one of the following options. You can't take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again. CHOSEN: Fighting Style: Dueling.

Second Wind: You have a limited well of stamina that you can draw on to protect yourself from harm. On your turn, you can use a bonus action to regain hit points equal to 1d10 + your fighter level. Once you use this feature, you must finish a short or long rest before you can use it again.
Fighting Style: Dueling: When you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls with that weapon.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.

Fighting Style: Dueling: When you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls with that weapon.

You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

sheet.name: Maren
sheet.opening: Maren stands in the courtyard of the Temple of the Anvil Father as evening shadows lengthen across the stone. The mine entrance was sealed at sunrise — she watched the masons lay the final bricks, heard the council's proclamation that the Old North Works were closed forever. Brakka never came back. They had served together for six years, shared meals in the refectory, traded stories of the mountain's moods. Now Brakka is gone, and Maren needs answers. Hessa is in her quarters, and Maren is heading there now, the miner's note burning in her mind — the one the miners left with the prior before they went down, warning of an old door that should never have been opened.
sheet.personality: I see omens in every event and action. The gods try to speak to us, we just need to listen. Nothing can shake my optimistic attitude.

Record new names and facts in your notebook with write_lore as you say them (hidden from the player); look things up with lore and recall before you state something you said earlier.

input.text:
The world is old, and the mountains remember everything that was ever buried in them. The Frostpeak range runs north to south like a wall of grey stone, and the people who live in its valleys have always dug into its bones for iron and silver. The Anvil Father, they say, forged the mountains themselves, and the dwarves who worship him have tended the deep places since before the humans came down from the north.

Brakka Ironvein is one of those dwarves. Six years ago she took the temple's oath and stood guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town carved into the western face of the Frostpeaks. She has kept the peace, watched the processions, and listened to the mountain groan through the stone walls. She knows the mine's sounds better than most.

Three days ago, three miners went down into the old north workings — tunnels sealed a generation ago after a collapse that no one in town likes to talk about. None of them came back. Last night a fourth man, Greth Oremine, stumbled out of the dark alone. He babbled about lights that walk and eyes that watch from deep stone, then died before dawn with his fingernails broken from clawing at the mine door.

Now Brakka stands at the mine mouth in the late afternoon light. The entrance is a mouth of rough-hewn stone, half-hidden by a wooden trestle and a rusted winch. Beyond it, the tunnel slopes downward into blackness. The lantern in her hand burns steady. The wind from below is cold and smells of wet stone and something else — something faintly metallic, like old blood on a blade.

Sunrise is tomorrow. After that, the council will seal the entrance forever.

What does Brakka do?

The ground at the mine mouth is hard-packed earth and gravel, but you find what you're looking for. Several sets of boot prints go in — three sets heading down three days ago, their strides even and purposeful. One set came back last night, the prints scuffed and stumbling, as if the man had been running blind. Beyond those, older prints are faint, half-buried under dust and time.

You tie your rope to the winch trestle, looping it twice and knotting it secure. Fifty feet of hempen rope should give you something to follow if the dark plays tricks on you.

Then you raise the lantern and step into the slope.

The tunnel descends at a steady angle, the walls rough-hewn stone that your darkvision picks out in shades of grey. The lantern casts warm light ahead of you, pushing back the blackness. Timber supports brace the ceiling at intervals, some old and black with age, others newer — the three miners must have replaced a few before they went deeper. The air is cold and damp, and that metallic smell grows stronger as you descend.

You walk for ten minutes, your boots echoing on the stone floor. The tunnel bends once to the left, then continues down. The rope trails behind you, a lifeline to the world above. Ahead, the light of your lantern reaches only so far before the dark swallows it.

You hear nothing but your own breathing and the drip of water somewhere in the distance.

What do you do?

You pick up the mining pick. It's heavy iron on a wooden handle, the kind used for breaking rock in tight spaces. You turn it in the lantern light, looking for blood, cracks, or signs of a struggle. The head is dull and pitted with age, the handle worn smooth by use. You don't see any blood or obvious damage. It looks like it was simply set down — or dropped in haste, though you can't tell which. You sling it over your shoulder; it might be useful, or its owner might need it found.

The scratch marks on the wall are another matter. You study them closely, running your fingers along the grooves. These are no accident. Someone made them deliberately, dragging a tool — likely that very pick — across the stone. They form rough arrows, all pointing deeper into the tunnel. But as you follow them, the marks change. The first few are neat, deliberate, spaced evenly. Further on, they grow closer together, the lines deeper, more jagged. Whoever made them was moving faster, pressing harder. The last set of scratches, about thirty feet ahead, ends in a deep gouge where the tool was driven into the wall and held there, as if the person leaned on it — or as if something made them stop suddenly.

The miners' prints continue past that point, but they're different now. The strides are shorter, closer together. And there are other marks in the dust — places where someone fell to their knees, then got up again.

The tunnel curves further left, descending more steeply. The air is colder, and that metallic taste is on your tongue now.

What do you do?

You move forward carefully, shield raised, lantern sweeping the walls and floor. At the deep gouge where the scratches end, you crouch and study the dust. Near the knee-marks, you find something: a small leather pouch, its drawstring pulled loose. Inside, you find a few copper pieces, a piece of chalk, and a folded note. The note reads, in a miner's rough hand: "Told ye we shouldn't have opened the old door. Hessa said seal it for a reason. But the vein runs deep and the council wants the ore." The note is dated three days ago.

You stand and look ahead. The tunnel continues its curve, and with your keen eyes you pick out what's been growing stronger: the walls here are different. Veins of a dark, almost black mineral run through the grey stone, branching like roots. The metallic smell comes from these veins — a sharp, iron-and-copper tang that coats your tongue. The mineral catches the lantern light with a faint, oily sheen, but it doesn't look like any ore you've seen in six years of guarding the temple's stores.

The miners' prints continue past the gouge, but they're erratic now — some steps forward, some back, as if the men had argued or panicked. Then, about forty feet ahead, the tunnel opens into a wider space. You can see where the old stonework ends and something else begins: a rough breach in the wall, as if someone had broken through into an older, natural cavern. Timber from the old seal lies splintered on the ground.

The air from that breach is colder, and the metallic smell is almost overpowering now. From somewhere beyond, you hear a sound — faint, but unmistakable. It's a low, rhythmic hum, like stone vibrating against stone.

You pocket the note and chalk, then mark a clear arrow at the gouge with the chalk. You creep toward the breach, keeping low and close to the wall, shield raised.

Your boot catches on a loose stone. It skitters across the floor with a sharp clatter that echoes down the tunnel. You freeze, but the damage is done — whatever is beyond that breach now knows you're here.

You edge to the breach and peer around it, holding your lantern low. Your keen eyes take in everything at once.

The cavern beyond is natural, not mined — a wide space with a low ceiling, its walls slick with moisture and veined with that same dark mineral. The air shimmers with the metallic smell, and the source of the hum is clear: three lights float in the cavern, each a pale blue-white globe about the size of a fist. They drift slowly, pulsing in rhythm, and where they pass near the walls, the dark veins glow faintly in response. The hum is their sound — a vibration that you feel in your teeth as much as hear.

But your eyes find something more important. Against the far wall, half-hidden in shadow, are two figures. Both are on their knees, their heads bowed, their hands clasped as if in prayer — but their eyes are open and blank, staring at nothing. The two living miners are breathing, but they don't respond to the lights that drift around them. One of the floating globes hovers just above the fallen miner, its light pulsing brighter.

The lights haven't noticed you yet — but they will, now that you've made noise.

What do you do?

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

Good question. There's a small problem: Brakka found the note in the mine, and she died down there with it. The mine was sealed at sunrise, so no one retrieved her body.

But here's a clean solution that keeps the clue in play: Brakka could have come back up briefly after finding the note, before going deeper. She might have brought it to Hessa as a report — "The miners opened an old door, and there's a note warning them to seal it." Hessa would have been alarmed. Then Brakka went back down to finish the search, and didn't come back.

After Brakka failed to return and the mine was sealed, Hessa would have kept the note as evidence. Now, with Brakka dead, Hessa gives it to Maren — the only person she trusts to understand what it means.

This requires a small retcon (Brakka came up briefly before going deeper), but it keeps the note in play and gives Maren a direct connection to the mystery. Does that work for you?

Evening shadows stretch across the courtyard of the Temple of the Anvil Father as Maren steps out of the refectory. The air is cold, carrying the scent of woodsmoke from the town below. The mine entrance was sealed at sunrise — she watched the masons lay the final bricks, heard the council's proclamation that the Old North Works were closed forever.

Brakka never came back.

They had served together for six years, shared meals in this very courtyard, traded stories of the mountain's moods. Brakka had gone down three days ago to find the missing miners, and yesterday Greth Oremine had stumbled out babbling about lights that walk. Then nothing. Now the mine is sealed, and Brakka is gone.

Hessa is in her quarters in the temple's east wing. The prior has been silent since the sealing, spending the day in prayer and contemplation. But Maren knows the old dwarf has answers — the miner's note that Hessa gave her this morning proves it. The miners had left it with the prior before they went down, warning that they shouldn't have opened the old door, that Hessa herself had said to seal it for a reason.

Maren's hand rests on the holy symbol at her chest. She needs to speak with Hessa, to understand what that door was, why it was sealed, and what took Brakka.

The temple's stone corridors are dim in the evening light, the lamps not yet lit. Hessa's quarters are down the east hall, past the shrine room where incense still burns.

What does Maren do?

You pause at the shrine room, touching the amulet at your chest. The incense hangs thick in the air, and the altar's single candle flickers as if breathing. You murmur a prayer for Brakka — for her soul to find the Anvil Father's forge, to be remade in stone and fire.

Then you continue down the east hall to Hessa's door. The wood is old, darkened with age and oil from many hands. You knock gently.

A moment passes. Then the door opens, and Hessa stands before you. She's smaller than you remember, or perhaps just more bent with grief. Her grey hair is unbound, falling past her shoulders, and her eyes are red-rimmed. She wears simple vestments, no ceremonial garb.

"Maren," she says, her voice rough. She steps back and opens the door wider. "Come in."

Her quarters are sparse — a narrow bed, a writing desk covered in papers and old books, a small shrine to the Anvil Father with a single unlit candle. The air smells of old paper and cold stone.

Hessa closes the door and turns to face you. Her eyes fall to the note in your hand.

"You've come about the door," she says. It's not a question.

She moves to her desk and sits heavily in a wooden chair, gesturing for you to sit on the bed. She folds her hands in her lap and looks at you for a long moment.

"Your friend Brakka went down there because I asked her to," Hessa says quietly. "The miners — Torvin, Durgan, and Kael — they went against my counsel. They'd found the old seal cracked, and they thought they could reopen the vein. I told them the door was sealed for a reason. But they wouldn't listen."

She pauses, her jaw tightening.

"Three days ago, they went down. Yesterday, Greth came back. He was... not right. He spoke of lights that walk, of a hum that gets inside your skull. Then he died in the night, his heart simply stopped."

Hessa's eyes meet yours.

"I sent Brakka to find them. To bring them back if she could. She didn't return. And now the council will seal the entrance at dawn."

She reaches into a drawer and pulls out a leather-bound book, old and worn. She sets it on the desk between you.

"The temple records go back eight generations," she says. "The door was sealed after the Collapse of the Deep Way. Miners broke through into an older cavern — natural, not carved. They found something there. Something that shouldn't have been disturbed. The records don't say what. Only that seventeen men went down, and only three came back. The survivors... they never spoke of what they'd seen. The door was sealed the next day."

She taps the book.

"There's more. The records mention a mineral — dark stone with an oily sheen. The miners called it 'blackvein.' It was found only in that cavern. The survivors said it sang to them. That it made the lights come."

Hessa leans forward.

"What did Brakka find down there, Maren? And is it still there?"

She turns another page. "There's mention of a ventilation shaft — an old one, carved to air out the cavern after the incident. It was sealed too, but less thoroughly. The records say it's 'above the old adit, behind the masonry.' The old adit is a smaller entrance higher up the mountain face, abandoned centuries ago. It's overgrown now, but it might still be passable."

Hessa looks up at you. "The records also say the survivors were found with their hands burned, as if they'd touched hot stone. And that the lights retreated when the temple priests came with consecrated oil and blessed the tunnel. The Anvil Father's light, they called it."

She closes the book and meets your eyes. "There's no map, Maren. No clear instructions. Only fragments. But if there's another way in, it's through that old adit. And if the lights fear the Anvil Father's light, then you'll need more than a lantern."

She stands and moves to her shrine, lighting the unlit candle. "Take this," she says, handing you a small vial of oil from the shrine. "It's been blessed. Consecrated to the Anvil Father. It won't last long, but it might buy you time."

She pauses, then adds, "The old adit is a two-hour climb up the mountain face from here. If you leave now, you might reach it before dawn."

Hessa nods solemnly. "I'll see to it, Maren. The Anvil Father go with you."

You pack the rope, the second lantern, the consecrated oil, and the miner's note. Your warhammer hangs at your belt, your light crossbow loaded and ready. You keep your shield close and move quietly, the metal gear muffled against your chain mail.

The climb is steep and cold. The path winds up the mountain face, switchbacking through scree and loose stone. The wind cuts through your cloak, and the stars above are sharp and bright in the winter sky. Your Guidance fades as you climb, but the Anvil Father's presence lingers in your mind.

After two hours of steady climbing, you reach the old adit. It's a narrow opening in the rock face, half-hidden by dead brush and lichen. The masonry Hessa mentioned is still there — old bricks, crumbling with age, sealing a ventilation shaft above the entrance. The wood of the original door frame is rotted away, and the stone around it is stained with moisture.

A figure waits nearby, huddled in a heavy cloak. He stands as you approach, his breath visible in the cold air.

"Maren?" he says. "I'm Dorin. Hessa sent word." His face is lined with worry, and his eyes keep moving toward the sealed entrance. "I've been up here before, checking the shafts. But I've never gone in. Not since... not since Torvin went down."

He gestures to the old adit. "The ventilation shaft is behind that masonry. It's narrow, but passable. It leads down to the cavern where... where they found the blackvein."
